title: Question 1.3
statement_text: Do there exist $c, \varepsilon > 0$ with the following property? Let $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, B_2, B_3)$ be a blockade in a graph $G$, and let $W$ be its width. If there is no $\mathcal{B}$-transversal triangle, then there exist distinct $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $X \subseteq B_i$ and $Y \subseteq B_j$, such that $X, Y$ is a pure pair, and $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. So a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal triangle is a triangle with one vertex in each of $B_1,B_2,B_3$. By a theorem of Erdős, Hajnal and Pach one always gets a pure pair with $|X|,|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$; the question asks for one side of linear size. It is a variant of a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov. Settling it was the authors' initial goal, but they could not; it is easy to reduce it to the sparse case where, for all distinct $i,j$, every vertex of $B_i$ has at most $|B_j|/100$ neighbours in $B_j$ (and 100 can be replaced by any number). A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. The authors prove that for every cycle $H$ of length $k\ge 4$ there are $\varepsilon,c>0$ such that every blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ of width $W$ with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ that is $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W^c)$-cohesive contains a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$; the same statement for $k=3$ is open and equivalent to this question.

title: Informal: which graphs H admit polynomial-size pure pairs
statement_text: For which ordered graphs $H$ can we get $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$ (for some $c, \varepsilon > 0$ depending only on $H$) as the pure pair conclusion, i.e. such that for every graph $G$ and every blockade $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, \ldots, B_{|H|})$ of width $W$ in $G$, either there is an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$, or there are distinct $i, j$ and $X \subseteq B_i$, $Y \subseteq B_j$ such that $X, Y$ is a pure pair with $|X| \geq \varepsilon W$ and $|Y| \geq \varepsilon W^c$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. An ordered graph is a graph $H$ with a fixed linear ordering $v_1,\dots,v_k$ of its vertices; an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$ in a blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ is a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy $J$ with an isomorphism $\phi:H\to J$ such that $\phi(v_i)\in B_i$ for all $i$. Erdős, Hajnal and Pach proved that for every ordered graph $H$ there exist $c,\varepsilon>0$ such that for every graph $G$ and every blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ of width $W$ with $k=|H|$, either there is an ordered $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$, or there are distinct $i,j$ and $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ forming a pure pair with $|X|,|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$. The authors ask for which $H$ one side of the pure pair can be made linear in $W$. Taking $c=1$ (both sides linear) is possible only for graphs $H$ with at most two vertices; the version with $|X|\ge\varepsilon W$ and $|Y|\ge\varepsilon W^c$ is called more promising. For $H$ a triangle this is an open question (a variant of a conjecture of Conlon, Fox and Sudakov). A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. In the sparse setting the paper gives partial answers: for every ordered tree $H$ with $k\ge 2$ vertices there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that every blockade of width $W$ with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ that is $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W^{1/(k-1)})$-cohesive contains an ordered transversal copy of $H$; for ordered caterpillars (trees whose vertices of degree more than one lie on one path) $W^{1/(k-1)}$ can be replaced by $W^{1/d}$ with $d$ the maximum degree of $H$, and for an ordered star with $t\ge 3$ leaves this fails for every exponent $c>1/t$.

title: Informal: characterization of graphs with the strong transversal property
statement_text: Which graphs $H$ have the strong transversal property, i.e., for which $H$ does there exist $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every graph $G$ with an $(\varepsilon W, \varepsilon W)$-cohesive blockade $\mathcal{B} = (B_1, \ldots, B_{|H|})$ of local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ contain a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple. A pure pair is a pair $X,Y$ of disjoint vertex sets that are complete (every vertex of $X$ adjacent to every vertex of $Y$) or anticomplete (no edges between them). A blockade $\mathcal{B}=(B_1,\dots,B_k)$ in $G$ is a sequence of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $V(G)$ (the blocks); its width $W$ is the minimum size of a block and its length is $k$. A copy of $H$ in $G$ is an induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$; it is $\mathcal{B}$-transversal if it has exactly one vertex in each block. A blockade has local degree $\lambda$ if $\lambda$ is the maximum, over distinct $i,j$ and $v\in B_i$, of the number of neighbours of $v$ in $B_j$; it is $(x,y)$-cohesive if for all distinct $i,j$ there are no $X\subseteq B_i$, $Y\subseteq B_j$ with $|X|\ge x$, $|Y|\ge y$ and $X$ anticomplete to $Y$. A graph $H$ has the strong transversal property if there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that for every graph $G$, every blockade $(B_1,\dots,B_{|H|})$ in $G$ of width $W$, with local degree less than $\varepsilon W$ and $(\varepsilon W,\varepsilon W)$-cohesive, contains a $\mathcal{B}$-transversal copy of $H$. A sparse random graph of large girth shows that such $H$ must be a forest, but not all forests have it. The authors prove: if every component of $H$ has the property so does $H$ (the converse is false); paths have it; a path with two extra vertices attached to its last vertex has it when $|H|>4$, and with $t$ extra vertices attached to its last vertex when $|H|>2^t(t^2-t+1)$; a path with three extra vertices attached to each end does not; and $H$ does not have it if it has a vertex of degree $d$ with $2^{d-1}\ge|H|$. In particular the property is not closed under induced subgraphs: the star $K_{1,3}$ fails it but adding an isolated vertex gives a forest that has it, and any forest gets the property after adding enough isolated vertices. No complete characterization is known.
